title: Roll Cameras!

paragraphs.text: Cinema is still widely regarded as a director's medium. However, the director relies heavily on the skills of the cinematographer - another name for the director of photography. The cinematographer's role is to help shape the film's narrative by using the camera in such a way that steers the audience's focus where the director wants them to be looking. Cinematographers have played a significant part in the history of cinema. However, the emphasis on the director as the prime creative force has meant that this contribution is not always recognised, nor the relationship between the two fully understood by the general public. Accomplished cinematographers have been central to developing the artistic style of many films, but balance is essential, and they also require specialist knowledge of mechanical and chemical processes related to their equipment. The close ties certain cinematographers have formed with high profile actresses have helped construct their on-screen image, including William Daniels with actress Greta Garbo. And cinematographers must be versatile; although individuals may have preferences for certain types of film, they need to possess the necessary skills to deal with the entire range of film genres.

In New Zealand, one of the pioneers of film-making was Rudall Hayward in the 1920s. Nonetheless, while there are interesting elements in this formative phase of New Zealand cinematography, the camera work is rarely anything other than plain and functional. Hayward's films rely on the kind of static photography that by this time was being superseded in other film-making nations by a more dynamic and mobile style of camera work.

In comparison, director John O'Shea's films represent a leap forward. The documentary style of Broken Barrier (1952), with cinematography by Roger Mirams, was a particular breakthrough. Despite the lack of any dialogue - the film was shot on two mute 35mm German Arriflex cameras O'Shea and Mirams achieve a beautiful and moving portrait of a landscape and its people that bears some comparison with the style that emerged in Italy in the late 1940s. Broken Barrier explores the possibilities of a harmonious New Zealand that bridges the gap between country and city, tradition and modernity.

The film-maker's ambitions are achieved through the use of many large close-ups, perhaps reflecting the beliefs of John Grierson, who said that 'every country has its own native genius, its own spirit, and it writes these on the faces of its people.' Even more interesting is O'Shea's second film, Runaway (1964). When the original cameraman pulled out, the job was given to 22-year-old Tony William. William had never photographed a film before, so he set about learning all he could by corresponding with fellow New Zealander John McGlashan, who was a cameraman in Britain. Assisted by the equally untested Michael Seresin, Williams amply rewarded O'Shea's faith in him, and Runaway has an accomplished visual style. Runaway opens with a group of fashionable young people swimming, sunbathing and waterskiing. This imagery of youth, leisure and freedom might have been commonplace on the French Riviera, but was previously unknown in a New Zealand context. Just as the opening of Broken Barrier suggests a certain kind of relationship between people and the seashore, so this scene sets a mood and tone that dictate the visual style of Runaway.

O'Shea's final feature film was Don't Let It Get You (1966). Made using the fast-paced, hand-held approach pioneered by some foreign films and TV series, O'Shea's musical is a collection of music video, documentary film footage, and dramatic episodes that follow the adventures of a struggling musician. While effectively photographed, the film lacks a strong narrative or even any plot to hold its parts together.

Since the 1970s, the New Zealand cinematographer has become a much more significant figure. In marked parallel with existing artistic traditions such as painting, the vast majority of New Zealand films have been set in the countryside or wilderness, exploring ideas of solitude, isolation and silence. Film-makers in New Zealand have also had to respond to one distinctive quality of the country's environment. As cinematographer Donny Duncan explains, '...if it's full sunshine on a clear day, and you wave your meter in the sun and then take a reading in the full shadow, the difference in the two readings is probably more extreme than anywhere on the planet. This unique contrast in the degree of brightness, which frequently occurs in New Zealand, has created a particular set of difficulties for the local cinematographer.

A number of other developments have contributed to a boom in New Zealand's film industry in recent decades. Early in his career the cinematographer Graeme Cowley became frustrated at the inadequacy of the production equipment available, and the problems of obtaining items such as a zoom lens or special tripod. Cowley came up with the idea of setting up businesses that would hire out film equipment, and eventually this proved beneficial to the whole industry. Another aspect of the film-making process is the laboratory where the film is developed. Most productions tended to use the National Film Unit laboratory, which suffered from a rather poor reputation. However, after a change of management the situation improved markedly. One other element of New Zealand film-making reflects the country's wider social structure. Camera crews in other parts of the world can be rigidly hierarchical and sometimes do not function well as a result. New Zealand crews, however, tend to be much more communal and collaborative, allowing them to work together more productively, which is one reason so many films are now made in the country.
